prompt: One player presses Jump 80 ms after leaving the edge. Another presses it 80 ms before landing. Which jumps happen?
rule: A platformer allows 100 ms of coyote time and remembers Jump for 100 ms before landing.

options.explanation: Coyote time handles the ledge, but buffering handles the landing too.
Both inputs fall inside their separate 100 ms windows.
The ledge input is also inside coyote time.

setupReplay.detail: Leave the edge → wait 80 ms → press Jump
Press Jump → wait 80 ms → land

resultReplay.detail: The ledge jump uses coyote time.
The landing jump uses the buffered input.

prompt: One holds Right. One holds Right + Up. Which trail is longer?
rule: Both characters move for the same time. Horizontal and vertical speeds are added separately; the direction is not normalised.

options.explanation: Adding two full axes produces a longer combined movement.
Normalising the direction would remove the diagonal speed advantage.
The straight input only uses one axis.

setupReplay.detail: Both characters start together.
One moves right; the other moves right and up.

resultReplay.detail: The diagonal character travels farther.
Normalise the input direction to keep the same speed.

prompt: Which camera motion matches the rule?
rule: The player changes lane immediately. Each update the camera moves one quarter of the remaining distance towards the player.

options.explanation: The remaining gap shrinks, so the steps shrink too.
Only the player snaps. The camera follows gradually.

options.text: Large first step, then smaller steps
options.explanation: Each camera step is a fraction of a progressively smaller gap.

setupReplay.detail: Player changes lane.

nodes.label: Camera follows ¼ of the gap each update

setupReplay.detail: Camera begins behind the new position.

nodes.label: Camera follows ¼ of the gap each update

resultReplay.detail: The camera moves quickly at first.

nodes.label: Camera follows ¼ of the gap each update

resultReplay.detail: It slows as it approaches the player.

nodes.label: Camera follows ¼ of the gap each update

prompt: What happens immediately after Left is held?
rule: The character has rightward velocity. Holding Left applies leftward acceleration; it does not set velocity directly.

options.explanation: Acceleration changes velocity over time.

options.text: It keeps moving right briefly, then reverses
options.explanation: Leftward acceleration first reduces the existing rightward velocity.
Continued acceleration eventually creates leftward velocity.

setupReplay.detail: Character is moving right.
Left input begins.

resultReplay.detail: Rightward movement slows.
The character then reverses to the left.

prompt: Which body pair fits both jobs?
rule: The train follows a scripted route and must not be pushed off it. Loose crates must fall and react to impacts.

options.explanation: A dynamic train may be pushed; static crates cannot fall.
A static train cannot follow a route, and kinematic crates do not fall under gravity.
Code controls the train while physics controls the crates.

setupReplay.detail: A train follows its route.
A loose crate falls into its path.

resultReplay.detail: The train continues its scripted motion.
The dynamic crate reacts to the collision.

prompt: Which change fixes the repeated boost?
rule: Jump should apply one impulse per press. The current code applies a new impulse on every physics tick while the button is held.

options.text: Apply the impulse only on the press edge
options.explanation: One press now produces one impulse.
Gravity changes the arc but leaves the repeated impulse bug.
Mass changes the response but does not stop repeated impulses.

setupReplay.detail: Jump is held over several physics ticks.
The current implementation keeps adding impulses.

resultReplay.detail: Detect a new press, not the held state.
Apply one impulse, then let gravity act.

prompt: How do their simulated jumps compare?
rule: Both phones use the same fixed physics step, starting state and physics-tick input. One renders at 30 FPS; the other at 120 FPS.

options.explanation: Render count does not change the fixed physics steps.

options.text: The same arc, with smoother rendering at 120 FPS
options.explanation: Equal physics steps and input produce the same simulated arc in this prototype.
The slower display does not add extra force.

setupReplay.detail: Both start with the same jump impulse.
Physics ticks equally; rendering rates differ.

resultReplay.detail: The simulated positions agree at each physics tick.
The faster screen shows more visual frames.

prompt: Compared with the original jump, what changes?
rule: Gravity is unchanged on the way up. It becomes stronger only after the jump reaches its apex.

options.explanation: Upward motion has already completed before the change.
The same ascent reaches the same peak; stronger falling gravity shortens descent.
Stronger gravity during descent cannot raise the completed peak.

setupReplay.detail: Both jumps rise with the same settings.

nodes.label: Gravity changes only after the apex

setupReplay.detail: At the apex, one switches to stronger gravity.

nodes.label: Gravity changes only after the apex

resultReplay.detail: Both reach the same peak.

nodes.label: Gravity changes only after the apex

resultReplay.detail: The modified jump falls and lands sooner.

nodes.label: Gravity changes only after the apex

rule: A swipe has one sample to the left of the fruit and the next to its right. Neither sample lies inside the fruit; their connecting segment crosses it.

options.text: Check only the two sample points
options.explanation: Both endpoints miss even though the swipe crosses the fruit.
Damage is applied after detection; it cannot repair a missed collision.

options.text: Check the segment between the samples
options.explanation: The segment covers the path travelled between samples.

setupReplay.detail: Sample 1 is outside the fruit.
Sample 2 is on the other side.

resultReplay.detail: The connecting segment crosses the fruit.
A segment test detects the slice.

prompt: A shot travels through water, past a teammate, then into a wall before the enemy. Where does it stop?
rule: In this prototype, shots pass over water and through teammates, but stop at solid walls.

options.explanation: Water blocks movement here, but not shots.
The wall is the first object on a blocking layer.
The wall stops the shot before it reaches the enemy.

setupReplay.detail: Shot → water → teammate
Then wall → enemy

resultReplay.detail: Water and teammate do not block it.
The wall stops it. The enemy is not hit.

prompt: How many hits should the attack produce?
rule: Only frames 3 and 4 have an active attack hitbox. The sword overlaps the target on frames 2 and 5 only.

options.explanation: Neither overlap happens during active attack frames.
A visible overlap alone does not create an active hitbox.
There is no overlap while the attack hitbox is active.

setupReplay.detail: Overlap on frame 2; active frames are 3–4.
Another overlap on frame 5.

resultReplay.detail: Frame 2 is wind-up; frame 5 is recovery.
Neither overlap produces damage.

rule: The player hurtbox is smaller than its sprite. The coin trigger extends beyond its artwork. The hazard touches only the player artwork; the coin trigger overlaps the player collider.

options.explanation: The hazard does not overlap the smaller hurtbox.
The enlarged coin trigger does overlap the player collider.
Collision shapes, rather than artwork edges, decide both outcomes.

setupReplay.detail: A hazard grazes the outer artwork.
The nearby coin trigger overlaps the player collider.

resultReplay.detail: The hazard misses the actual hurtbox.
The pickup trigger collects the coin.
